opus_only: A model is judged by the usefulness and accuracy of its predictions, not by whether it is "true".
Tiny discrepancies between a near-true theory and observations can have enormous consequences (Newton to Einstein).
Natural experiments in economics take long and are less conclusive than controlled experiments.
Unlike physics, markets consist of thinking agents who react, which makes economic modelling harder.
Models are best judged on data that arrived after they were built (no prior knowledge), i.e. genuine out-of-sample tests over long periods.
Trying to beat the market is a rigorous scientific test, not just a desire for money.
Other models are equally consistent with the difficulty of making money, so this is not unique support for EMH.
Wide adoption of a financial theory shows it is marketable, not that it is scientifically useful.
Rocket-scientist arbitrage works because EMH-based models are robust for relative values, though its assumptions may be unsound.
The speculator's method: observe and classify market phenomena, then build models by analogy that make interesting falsifiable predictions.
EMH has partly removed charlatans, opening the field to scientists.
sonnet_only: Empirical testing gives an independent way to arbitrate between views, replacing sterile conflict with constructive argument.
Ultimate test of a model's utility is profit from exploiting differences between its predictions and common opinion; older models are easier to judge because social systems evolve slowly.
Efficient market theory denies that speculators can exist, so speculators who succeed conflict with it.
